TOP STORY

Bitcoin ripped back to eight-month highs on the back of a brutal short squeeze while Washington's crypto rulebook stayed exactly as unwritten as it was last week.

stories.headline: Bitcoin Tops $85K, Mostly by Force
stories.body:
Bitcoin cracked $85,000 for the first time since January, and the move had less to do with a wave of new buyers than with traders on the wrong side of the bet getting steamrolled. Decrypt reports $648 million in crypto shorts were liquidated as the squeeze kicked off, though spot buyers reportedly kept the rally going afterward, with one measure of selling pressure sitting near a record low.

A short squeeze can look identical to genuine conviction for a few hours, which is exactly the problem with using price alone as a mood ring. Worth remembering that 'the shorts got wrecked' and 'the market believes in this' are two different sentences, even when the candle looks the same.

stories.headline: Congress Fumbles Clarity Act, So the Regulators Grabbed the Wheel
stories.body:
The Clarity Act failed to advance in the Senate, and rather than crypto policy going dormant, the action just moved venues. Decrypt notes the industry's focus has shifted to a fresh wave of activity from the SEC and CFTC, who are apparently not waiting around for lawmakers to agree on anything.

This is the classic Washington shuffle: when the legislative branch can't get its act together, the alphabet-soup agencies fill the vacuum with rulemaking that nobody voted on directly. Good for near-term clarity, maybe, but it also means the rules of the road can shift again the next time the political wind changes.

stories.headline: Strategy Keeps Stacking, Now at 4% of All Bitcoin That Will Ever Exist
stories.body:
Strategy added another 950 bitcoin for roughly $76 million, pushing its total holdings to about 846,000 BTC — around 4% of the entire 21 million supply cap, worth roughly $72 billion according to The Block.

At this point Strategy isn't really a bitcoin buyer so much as a permanent structural feature of the market, which raises an interesting question nobody seems eager to answer out loud: what happens to bitcoin's supply dynamics when one company owns a chunk this large? Not a crisis, necessarily, but definitely a variable worth tracking rather than ignoring.

stories.headline: The ECB Builds Its Own Tokenization Rails, Skips the Stablecoin Middleman
stories.body:
The European Central Bank launched Pontes, a platform for settling tokenized assets using central-bank money instead of stablecoins, with plans to expand its services and operating hours over time, per Cointelegraph.

Notice what's missing from that sentence: any private stablecoin issuer. Central banks watching stablecoins eat into their turf were never going to just shrug about it, and Pontes looks like Europe's answer — take the tokenization efficiency crypto proved out, wire it directly to the central bank's own money instead of letting a private company sit in the middle.

stories.headline: France Remains the World's Worst Place to Be a Visible Crypto Holder
stories.body:
A grim reminder that this industry has a physical-world crime problem: Decrypt reports a French crypto worker's children were held hostage in the latest 'wrench attack,' with $46,000 taken. France is the worst-hit country globally for these attacks, logging more than 70 in the first eight months of 2026 alone.

No clever take here, just a plain observation — the more visibly wealthy this industry gets, the more it needs to think about operational security in the boring, unglamorous sense: who knows you hold crypto, and what have you done to make that information harder to find.

stories.headline: Zcash's ETF Is So Popular It Needs a Stock Split
stories.body:
Grayscale's Zcash ETF is splitting shares 3-for-1 to make itself more affordable after pulling in more than $233 million in under a month, Decrypt reports, as Wall Street piles into what's being called crypto's hottest privacy trade.

It's a genuinely funny twist of the cycle: an asset built explicitly around shielding transaction details from view is now one of the most closely watched, publicly reported line items in traditional finance. Privacy coins finding their moment inside the most transparent wrapper imaginable — a public ETF ticker — is the kind of irony this industry seems to specialize in.

stories.headline: Gemini's Stock Is Down 80%, and the Rumor Mill Loves It
stories.body:
Gemini's stock has fallen 80% from its IPO price, and CoinDesk reports that slide is reviving takeover speculation across the industry.

A public listing was supposed to be the victory lap; instead it's become a discount sticker that other players are reportedly eyeing. It's a useful case study in how 'going public' doesn't automatically mean 'derisking' — sometimes it just means your struggles are now quoted in real time, for everyone to see.
